text: One might object that the chapter merely follows the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains it. There is some truth in this. But the same writer reports feeling freely enough elsewhere: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate, and a writer who could have said what was felt, as he says it of Esau and Joseph, and chose silence instead, means that silence as an accusation.
